final_recommendation: The room converged on a Protocol of Amendment to be signed by Friday, locking in enforceable labor enforcement mechanisms (20% monthly facility audits, trilateral auditor appointment, automatic day-5 tariff snapback at 5% violation threshold, 10-day publication and 5-day validation timelines) with explicit carve-outs protecting dairy schedules and tariff rates from reopening. Congress commits to a Friday markup vote contingent on Mexico's signature; business commits to full ratification push; Mexico commits to sign with no further conditions.
key_conflicts: Mexico's sovereignty concern over U.S.-controlled auditor vs. joint trilateral appointment
Congress demand for Protocol amendment text vs. Mexico's initial preference for side letter
Canada's fear that formal amendment would reopen dairy concessions
Labor union insistence on enforceable timelines in treaty text vs. risk of implementation memo slippage
key_concessions: Mexico accepted automatic tariff snapback with no appeals process in exchange for trilateral auditor appointment and sovereignty over inspection process
U.S. Congress accepted joint trilateral auditor (not unilateral U.S. control) to secure Mexico's signature
Business lobby accepted formal Protocol amendment (not just side letter) to secure Congressional votes
All parties accepted explicit carve-outs locking dairy and tariff schedules outside amendment scope to secure Canada's participation
red_lines: Congress: no vote without enforceable snapback mechanism in Protocol text itself (not side letter or implementation memo)
Mexico: no signature if U.S. unilaterally controls auditor or if amendment reopens tariff schedules
Canada: no signature if formal amendment process risks reopening dairy concessions
Labor: no support if enforcement timelines (publication, validation) slip into post-ratification implementation procedures
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Political risk that automatic tariff snapback could trigger U.S.-Mexico trade conflict if violations are found
Implementation risk: whether 20% monthly facility coverage is operationally feasible for Mexico's labor inspectorate
Domestic political risk in Mexico: whether automatic tariff exposure on Mexican exports is defensible to Mexican industry and public
Timeline risk: whether all three countries can finalize legal text, secure signatures, and schedule Congressional vote within 48-72 hours
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Mexico's labor inspectorate can operationally deliver 20% monthly facility coverage and 10-day publication timeline
Whether the trilateral auditor appointment process becomes a new point of friction or delay
Whether the automatic snapback mechanism survives first contact with actual violations (political pressure to waive or delay)
Whether Canadian domestic opposition to dairy concessions resurfaces during ratification despite carve-out language
Whether business lobby's ratification push can overcome residual Congressional skepticism about enforcement credibility
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved formal convergence on Protocol text and Friday signature/vote timeline, but left unresolved: (1) operational feasibility of Mexico's inspection and publication commitments, (2) political durability of automatic snapback if violations are actually found, (3) whether 48-hour drafting and signature timeline is realistic, (4) whether labor unions will actually endorse the final text or remain skeptical of enforcement credibility despite locked timelines.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress opened with 'I've got the votes to kill this thing' and repeatedly demanded enforceable Protocol text as precondition for markup vote; ratification risk drove every major concession and the entire amendment path.
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor union's insistence on 'actual enforcement mechanism—independent inspectors, real penalties' and detailed timelines (10-day publication, 5-day validation, 20% coverage) drove the Protocol architecture and was central to every round.
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business committed to 'full ratification push' contingent on Friday Protocol signature and repeatedly pressed for timeline certainty, but did not dominate the room's direction—accepted amendment path to secure Congressional votes.
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada's repeated insistence on explicit carve-out language protecting dairy concessions was a genuine constraint that shaped the Protocol scope, but was resolved mid-meeting and did not drive the overall trajectory.
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico's concern over U.S.-controlled auditor ('that's not enforcement of Mexican law, that's U.S. surveillance') was a real negotiating point that forced trilateral auditor compromise, but was resolved and did not dominate the room.
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor framed the public narrative ('workers get to watch whether this actually holds') and pushed for transparency timelines, but was reactive to the room's direction rather than driving it.
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: The entire meeting was premised on the understanding that the original USMCA package could not pass as-is and required a Protocol amendment to achieve ratification—this was the foundational assumption driving all negotiation.
